rows.subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
rows.description: A young child's shaking may reflect cold, fear, excitement or tiredness. Warmth and calm closeness address most causes, and a persistent tremor is a matter for a doctor.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: affection, fear, excitement, tiredness

rows.description: A preschooler wails theatrically over a small bump or squeals with over-large delight. Exaggeration often seeks attention or shows big feelings without control, and a calm response teaches proportion.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A young child takes words at face value, such as hearing it is raining cats and dogs and looking for animals. Direct plain language is clearest for this age.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A preschooler laughs nervously after being caught doing something wrong or being teased. The laugh is discomfort, not amusement, and a kind tone helps the child feel safe.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 7–12, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: amusement, anxiety, embarrassment, trust

rows.subtype: Hiding a grimace to be polite [Regulating]
rows.description: A child learns to swallow a grimace at an unwanted gift or unpleasant food to avoid hurting someone. This display rule is a social skill, though constant hiding of real distress from trusted adults is worth gently noticing.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
rows.description: A school-age child notices a classmate's smirk or sneer and reads possible mockery or superiority, though the same look can be nervousness. Asking or watching more context is wiser than assuming an insult.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A school-age child gives a small closed-mouth smile when meeting new people, often carrying shyness or politeness rather than delight. Giving time and not forcing a bigger smile respects temperament.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: joy, admiration, shyness

rows.description: A child smiles nervously while being told off, which may signal fear, embarrassment or a wish to calm the adult, not amusement. Adults who read it as cheek risk punishing a frightened child.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
related mind states: amusement, fear, anxiety, embarrassment

rows.description: A child furrows the brow over a maths problem, which peers may misread as anger at them. Explaining that the face means thinking can prevent needless friction.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26

rows.description: A school-age child sees a teacher raise one eyebrow and reads doubt, questioning or mild disapproval. Reading it as a question and offering an explanation works better than assuming anger.
graph_context: this subtopic also appears at ages: 1–3, 4–6, 13–17, 18–22, 23–26
